lede: Counting, summing and finding the biggest value per key is the core of most reports. On RDDs you do it with pairs: a key and a value, combined per key with `reduceByKey`.
objectives: Build a pair RDD of `(key, value)` tuples with `map`
Combine the values of each key with `reduceByKey`, and change only values with `mapValues`
Carry several numbers at once in a tuple, for counts, sums and averages
Explain why `reduceByKey` beats `groupByKey`, and sort pair results for stable output

blocks.md: `api_requests` has one row per API call: which service answered, the HTTP status, and the latency in milliseconds. To work per service, turn each row into a **pair**: a Python tuple `(key, value)`. An RDD of pairs gets extra methods that work per key.

blocks.title: Rows into pairs
blocks.code:
pairs = api_requests.rdd.map(lambda r: (r["service"], r["latency_ms"]))
print(pairs.take(4))
print(pairs.keys().take(4))
print(pairs.values().take(4))
blocks.note: Each item is a two-item tuple. `keys()` and `values()` take the first or second part of every pair.

blocks.md:
`reduceByKey(f)` combines all the values of one key, two at a time, with a function `f(a, b)` that returns one value of the same kind. `lambda a, b: a + b` adds them up; `max` keeps the bigger. The result has one pair per key.

Pair results come back in no particular order: they've been shuffled between partitions to bring each key together. Sort what you collect, with Python's `sorted` or with `sortByKey()`, whenever the order matters.

blocks.title: Count and find the maximum per key
blocks.code:
counts = api_requests.rdd.map(lambda r: (r["service"], 1)).reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b)
print(sorted(counts.collect()))

slowest = api_requests.rdd.map(lambda r: (r["service"], r["latency_ms"])).reduceByKey(max)
print(slowest.sortByKey().collect())
blocks.note: Counting is adding a 1 per row. catalog-api answered 5 of the 12 calls. The slowest call was checkout-api's 1240 ms payment failure.

blocks.md:
The function must give the same answer whatever order the values arrive in, because Spark combines them inside each partition first and then combines the partial results. Adding, `max` and `min` are safe. Taking an average isn't: the average of two averages isn't the average of all values.

To average, carry a tuple of **(sum, count)**, add both parts in `reduceByKey`, and divide at the end. `mapValues(f)` changes only the value of each pair and keeps the key.

blocks.title: An average via (sum, count)
blocks.code:
sums = (
    api_requests.rdd
    .map(lambda r: (r["service"], (r["latency_ms"], 1)))
    .reduceByKey(lambda a, b: (a[0] + b[0], a[1] + b[1]))
)
print(sorted(sums.collect()))

averages = sums.mapValues(lambda s: round(s[0] / s[1], 1))
print(sorted(averages.collect()))
blocks.note: search-api had two calls, 118 and 162 ms: (280, 2), an average of 140.0. The same tuple trick carries any number of counters at once.

blocks.md: `groupByKey()` collects every value of a key into one list-like group. It's handy for looking, but costly: every value travels across the network before anything is combined. `reduceByKey` combines values in each partition first and sends only the partial results, so for sums, counts and maximums it does far less work. Reach for `groupByKey` only when you really need all the values together.

blocks.title: groupByKey gives all the values
blocks.code:
groups = api_requests.rdd.map(lambda r: (r["service"], r["status_code"])).groupByKey()
print(sorted((service, sorted(codes)) for service, codes in groups.collect()))
blocks.note: Each group is an iterable of every status code for that service; `sorted` turns it into a plain list for printing. catalog-api's 404 sits among its 200s.

blocks.md: Finish as usual by turning pairs into rows. A pair whose value is a tuple has to be flattened into one tuple per row first, then `toDF` with a schema string.

blocks.title: Pairs back to a DataFrame
blocks.code:
stats = (
    api_requests.rdd
    .map(lambda r: (r["service"], (1, 1 if r["status_code"] >= 500 else 0)))
    .reduceByKey(lambda a, b: (a[0] + b[0], a[1] + b[1]))
    .sortByKey()
    .map(lambda kv: (kv[0], kv[1][0], kv[1][1]))
)
stats.toDF("service string, requests bigint, server_errors bigint").show()
blocks.note: One row per service with two counters. Only checkout-api had a 5xx error. `sortByKey()` before the last `map` puts the services in order, and `toDF` keeps that order.

blocks.title: reduceByKey on items that aren't pairs
blocks.code:
services = api_requests.rdd.map(lambda r: r["service"])
print(services.reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b).collect())
blocks.note: Each item is a plain string, not a `(key, value)` tuple, so Spark can't split it into a key and a value. Python's unpacking error is inside the long Spark message. Map to pairs first: `map(lambda r: (r["service"], 1))`.

concept.prompt: Which function is safe to use with `reduceByKey` to find the total latency per service?
concept.why: Adding gives the same total whatever order values are combined in. Averaging pairwise does not, keeping `a` depends on order, and a list changes the kind of value.

concept.prompt: Why prefer `reduceByKey` to `groupByKey` for counting requests per service?
choices: `reduceByKey` combines values inside each partition before the shuffle, so far less data moves
concept.why: Both can count correctly, but `groupByKey` ships every value across the network first; `reduceByKey` sends only partial results.

choices: Doubles each value and keeps its key
concept.why: `mapValues` applies the function to the value of each pair and leaves the key as it is.

review: A pair RDD holds `(key, value)` tuples; build one with `map(lambda r: (key, value))`.
`reduceByKey(f)` combines a key's values two at a time; `f` must not depend on the order (adding, `max`, `min`).
Average with `(sum, count)` tuples, then divide in `mapValues`.
`groupByKey` moves every value before combining; prefer `reduceByKey` for sums, counts and maximums.
Pair results have no fixed order: sort with `sorted(...)` or `sortByKey()` when it matters.
Flatten `(key, (a, b))` into `(key, a, b)` before `toDF("...")`.
